extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of Montaigne; patrons, scholars, and general literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Early‑modern dedicatory prefaces and private/public letters: rhetorical conventions for presenting works to patrons, recommending persons, commemorating the dead, and petitioning officials. Contains norms about humility, selection of material, and modes of praise and recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present the work under the patron’s auspices
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is only right, Monseigneur, that the work should come before the world under your auspices," (i.e. present the translated/emended work as issued under the protection/authority of the patron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the patron’s name/auspices to give the work authority and credibility; attribute emendations and polish to the patron to enhance reception and justify publication under their protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute improvements to the patron and display humility
rubrics_metrics.description: “whatever emendations and polish it may have received, are owing to you.” — When presenting a work, stress that any improvements are due to the patron, not the translator/editor alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt modest phrasing about your own competence; emphasize patron’s contribution to deflect criticism and flatter the dedicatee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a dedicatee appropriate to the work’s content
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a recipient whose interests or station make the gift fitting (e.g. present a household-management text to a lady of the house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain specifically why the recipient is suitable (social rank, personal tastes, past acquaintance), so the dedication appears thoughtful and not random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and publish the memory of the dead as a duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent worthy names and memories from "falling into oblivion" by collecting and publishing their remains and works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather scattered papers, select materials that best show the deceased’s qualities, and present them publicly to keep their reputation and example alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false or undeserved praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The text warns that "the vice of falsehood is one very unbecoming in a gentleman" and that bestowing reputation without cause is pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise should be truthful and supported by knowledge; avoid flattery for its own sake since undeserved praise damages credibility and the practice of commendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use praise as a stimulant to the living
rubrics_metrics.description: "The custom of praising virtue... serves as a stimulant to the living to imitate their example."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commemorating others, frame praise as having social utility — to encourage virtuous conduct in the living — not merely as private flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: When recommending clemency or favour, present mitigating facts and personal testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: In petitions (e.g., for a prisoner), set out the act in context, argue why it was excusable or commendable, and provide personal acquaintance and character references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply concrete facts, evidence of the person’s past good conduct, relationship to you, and a reasoned moral/political argument for leniency to influence decision‑makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address officials with deference, concision, and reminders of mutual interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters to magistrates and sovereigns repeatedly use humble forms ("I pray God to grant you... Your humble servant") and briefly state the purpose, grounds, and expected public advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deferential in tone, concise in purpose, and connect the petition or information to the public good or the recipient’s duties to make the appeal appropriate and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge imperfections and select the best from scattered material
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing an assemblage of another’s fragments, admit the roughness ("green wood and dry") and choose the pieces most likely to represent the author's worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be candid about the incomplete/crude nature of collected materials while deliberately selecting the strongest examples to support your purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clemency and generosity in governance to secure long‑term allegiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Political counsel: "it is better that you be beloved rather than feared... clemency and generosity [are] excellent lures to draw men to the just and legitimate side."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that mercy and magnanimity after conquest or dispute win durable loyalty; recommend delaying severity until success is secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publication and presentation to repay obligations and perform service
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer books or publications as tokens of service when one cannot give something else of value: "in default of better coin, I offer you in payment the assurance of my desire to do you humble service."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing a gift as an expression of personal obligation or desire to serve makes it a fitting social currency in patronage contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground strong commendations in intimate knowledge of the person
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming extraordinary qualities for a deceased friend, stress close and continuous acquaintance as the basis for testimony: "I was so nearly a prodigy... I am afraid of not being credited..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear your direct observations and longstanding relationship to lend weight to exceptional praise; anticipate skepticism and preempt it with disclosure of proximity and evidence.
